name: Rate Limiting
shortDef: A mechanism that controls how quickly a client, user, or service can consume an API or other shared resource, protecting capacity and enforcing quotas.
fullDef:
## What rate limiting actually does

Rate limiting is an admission-control mechanism. It defines how much work a caller is allowed to start over some period instead of allowing every request to compete for resources immediately. The limit may be expressed as requests per second, requests per minute, tokens per minute, concurrent requests, bytes per second, or another unit that maps to the scarce resource.

The important design question is not simply "how many requests can this client make?" It is "which resource are we protecting, and what kind of overload are we trying to prevent?" A model API may need a request-per-minute limit as well as a token-per-minute limit because ten short requests and ten enormous prompts do not consume the same capacity.

## Common algorithms

A **fixed-window** limiter counts requests inside discrete windows such as 10:00:00–10:00:59. It is easy to implement, but a client can burst at the boundary between two windows. A **sliding-window** approach reduces this boundary effect by considering a moving time range.

A **token bucket** starts with a bucket containing tokens. Tokens are replenished at a configured rate up to a maximum capacity, and each request consumes one or more tokens. This gives a useful combination of an average rate limit and a controlled burst allowance. A **leaky bucket** instead behaves more like a queue draining at a fixed rate. The two are often discussed together because both smooth traffic, but they produce different burst semantics.

## Where the limit lives

Limits can be enforced at an API gateway, load balancer, application server, service mesh, or downstream resource itself. They can be keyed by IP, API key, authenticated user, tenant, endpoint, model, organization, or combinations of those dimensions. In multi-instance systems, a purely local counter means every replica gets its own quota. That can unintentionally multiply a supposedly global limit, so distributed deployments may use a shared store, a gateway-level limiter, or an approximate algorithm with bounded error.

A rejected request commonly receives HTTP 429. The response can include `Retry-After` or another hint so well-behaved clients know when to try again. The goal is to make overload explicit instead of allowing latency to grow until requests simply time out.

## Rate limiting is not enough

A client can stay under a request-rate limit and still overload a system through expensive concurrency, huge payloads, long-lived streams, or memory-heavy operations. That is why production systems usually combine rate limiting with **concurrency limits, backpressure, queue bounds, timeouts, and observability**.

There is also a product trade-off. A limit that is too aggressive produces false rejections and a poor developer experience. A limit that is too generous is effectively useless. Good limits are based on measured capacity, tenant behavior, and the cost of the protected operation rather than arbitrary round numbers.

## Example

Imagine an LLM API that can safely process 200 requests per second but only 2 million input tokens per minute. A tenant might be allowed 100 requests per second while also receiving a 500,000-token-per-minute budget. One limit protects request overhead; the other protects compute and memory consumed by large prompts.

## The core idea

Rate limiting is about **controlling admission before the system becomes saturated**. It is a deliberate refusal to let demand grow faster than the system's capacity can safely absorb.
analogy: Like a nightclub controlling how quickly people enter so the room never fills faster than staff can safely serve it.
seoDescription: Rate limiting controls request frequency to protect APIs and distributed systems from overload, enforce quotas, and keep resource usage predictable.

name: Kubernetes
shortDef: An open-source orchestration system that schedules and manages containerized workloads across clusters, automating placement, health, networking, and lifecycle operations.
fullDef:
## What Kubernetes is

Kubernetes is a container orchestration system built around a **declarative control model**. You describe the state you want—such as three replicas of an API, a particular container image, resource limits, and health checks—and Kubernetes continuously works to make the running cluster resemble that desired state.

This is fundamentally different from treating deployment as a one-time script. Machines fail, Pods disappear, nodes become unavailable, images change, and capacity moves around. Kubernetes is designed for a world where the underlying infrastructure is constantly changing.

## The core objects

A **Pod** is the basic scheduling unit and contains one or more tightly coupled containers. A **Deployment** manages replicated, usually stateless workloads and coordinates rolling updates. A **Service** provides stable discovery and networking in front of Pods whose individual identities can change. **ConfigMaps** and **Secrets** separate configuration and sensitive values from container images. **Jobs** and **CronJobs** model finite or scheduled work, while **StatefulSets** provide stable identity and ordering behavior for stateful applications.

The control plane watches the cluster and runs controllers that reconcile actual state toward desired state. On each node, the kubelet is responsible for making sure assigned Pods are actually running. The scheduler chooses nodes based on resource requirements, constraints, affinities, taints, and other rules.

## Why it matters for serving

For APIs and model-serving systems, Kubernetes provides a common operating substrate for replication, health checks, rolling deployments, resource isolation, service discovery, and scaling. A model server can be represented as a Deployment, exposed by a Service, and scaled based on traffic or queue pressure. Readiness checks can prevent a freshly started worker from receiving traffic before its model is loaded.

That last detail is important. A process being alive does not mean it is ready to serve. Kubernetes lets teams distinguish liveness from readiness, which becomes valuable for slow-starting inference workers and cache-heavy services.

## What Kubernetes does not solve

Kubernetes does not automatically make an application fast, cheap, or reliable. It introduces its own control-plane, scheduling, networking, storage, and operational complexity. A small service may be easier to run on a VM or a managed application platform.

It also does not remove the need for good application architecture. If a database becomes the bottleneck, adding more Pods does not fix the database. If a service retries aggressively, Kubernetes will happily give you more replicas that may all participate in the same retry storm.

## The core idea

Kubernetes is best understood as a **continuous reconciliation system for distributed workloads**. Its power comes from making deployment, recovery, placement, and scaling repeatable across a fleet rather than relying on manual intervention on individual machines.
analogy: Like a warehouse manager that continuously decides where inventory should go, replaces damaged stock, and keeps the warehouse in the state you requested.
seoDescription: Kubernetes is a declarative container orchestration system for scheduling, scaling, networking, and healing workloads across clusters.

name: Autoscaling
shortDef: The automatic adjustment of compute capacity in response to changing workload demand, balancing performance, availability, and infrastructure cost.
fullDef:
## What autoscaling means

Autoscaling is a feedback loop that changes available compute capacity as workload demand changes. Instead of running a fixed number of workers at all times, a system observes one or more load signals and increases or decreases capacity according to a policy.

The objective is not "use as few machines as possible." It is to maintain acceptable performance and availability while avoiding capacity that sits idle. That creates a three-way trade-off between **latency, headroom, and cost**.

## Horizontal vs vertical scaling

**Horizontal scaling** changes the number of instances. It works well for stateless APIs because requests can be spread across replicas. **Vertical scaling** changes the size of an instance by giving it more CPU, memory, or accelerator capacity. Stateful databases and some specialized workloads may rely more heavily on vertical scaling.

Horizontal autoscalers usually maintain a target metric. If observed utilization remains above target, additional replicas are created; if it remains below target, capacity is removed. Cooldowns and stabilization windows are important because a noisy metric can otherwise cause the system to oscillate between scale-up and scale-down.

## Choosing the signal

The best signal is usually the metric closest to the real saturation point. CPU is useful for CPU-bound services but can be misleading for an LLM server where the bottleneck is GPU memory, queue time, or active generation slots. Queue depth is often a strong signal for asynchronous workers because it represents demand waiting for capacity. Concurrency can be useful when each in-flight request consumes a predictable amount of scarce resources.

Latency can be used as an outcome signal, but scaling directly on noisy latency measurements can create unstable feedback. The system may add capacity after latency has already exploded, then remove it too quickly after a short recovery.

## Scaling is not instant

A new instance has a startup delay. The machine may need to boot, the container image may need to download, dependencies may initialize, and a model may need to load into GPU memory. This means an autoscaler reacting perfectly to the present can still respond too late to a sudden spike.

Production systems compensate with **minimum warm capacity, prewarming, scheduled scaling, predictive scaling, queue-aware scaling, and admission control**. The goal is to have enough capacity available before the next burst becomes user-visible.

## Example

Suppose an inference service has eight warm GPU workers and traffic normally uses six. During a launch, queue depth rises rapidly. The autoscaler adds four workers, but each takes 40 seconds to load the model. If demand spikes for only 20 seconds, scaling cannot rescue the first wave of requests. Keeping two extra warm workers may therefore cost more but produce a much better latency profile.

## The core idea

Autoscaling is a control problem. The hard part is not creating another VM; it is choosing signals, thresholds, cooldowns, and headroom so that the system reacts quickly enough without constantly chasing noise.
analogy: Like opening more checkout counters when the line grows, while remembering that a new cashier still needs time to arrive and get ready.
seoDescription: Autoscaling adjusts compute capacity as demand changes, balancing latency and availability against infrastructure cost and scaling delay.

name: Backpressure
shortDef: A flow-control mechanism that makes downstream capacity visible to upstream producers, preventing work queues and resource usage from growing without bound.
fullDef:
## The problem backpressure solves

Suppose a producer can generate 10,000 work items per second while the consumer can process only 4,000. Something must absorb the difference. If the system simply keeps accepting work, memory fills, queues grow, threads wait, connections accumulate, and eventually the process or downstream dependency fails. **Backpressure makes the consumer's limited capacity visible to the producer.**

Instead of saying "keep sending and we will figure it out later," a backpressured system says "slow down, wait, or stop because the downstream stage cannot safely accept more work right now."

## How it is implemented

A **bounded queue** can stop accepting new items once it reaches capacity. A streaming system can use demand signals or window sizes so a producer sends only what a consumer has requested. A synchronous API can block briefly, reject work, or return an overload response. Message brokers can apply consumer-side flow control, while TCP implements a low-level form of backpressure through receive windows.

The exact mechanism differs, but the principle is the same: **do not allow an unconstrained upstream rate to overwhelm a constrained downstream stage.**

## Backpressure vs rate limiting

The concepts are related but not identical. Rate limiting is usually a configured admission budget: a client may make 100 requests per second. Backpressure is a response to current capacity: the consumer cannot keep up, so production must slow down now.

A system can therefore have a 100-requests-per-second rate limit and still require backpressure because those 100 requests might all become expensive concurrent operations at once. Rate limiting protects capacity from excessive callers; backpressure protects a pipeline from downstream saturation.

## What happens when the buffer fills?

A bounded system must eventually choose a policy. It can **wait**, **reject**, **drop low-priority work**, **sample**, or **persist work for later**. The correct answer depends on the product. An analytics pipeline might safely drop old events. A payment system should not silently drop work. An interactive LLM request might be better rejected quickly than allowed to sit in a queue for two minutes.

This is why unbounded queues are dangerous. They can turn overload into seemingly successful acceptance while silently converting it into enormous latency.

## Example

Consider token streaming from a model server. If clients read slowly and the server continues generating into an unlimited per-client buffer, memory usage can grow with every slow connection. A bounded buffer forces the system to slow generation, pause the producer, or terminate the stream according to policy.

## The core idea

Backpressure is **controlled flow through a system whose stages have different capacities**. It prevents overload by making it impossible—or at least deliberately difficult—for upstream demand to grow without regard for downstream limits.
analogy: Like a kitchen that stops accepting orders when the cooks are overwhelmed instead of stacking tickets until the whole restaurant collapses.
seoDescription: Backpressure prevents overloaded consumers from being overwhelmed by controlling how quickly upstream systems produce work.

name: Streaming / SSE
shortDef: A pattern for delivering results incrementally over a long-lived connection; Server-Sent Events (SSE) provides HTTP-based server-to-client event streaming.
fullDef:
## What streaming changes

A traditional request/response API waits until the server has the complete result and then returns one payload. **Streaming** changes that contract: the server sends pieces as they become available. This is especially important for generative AI, where the first few tokens can be produced long before the final answer is complete.

Streaming therefore improves **time to useful output**, not necessarily total computation time. A model that needs 8 seconds to finish still needs roughly 8 seconds of compute even if the first token arrives after 300 ms.

## Server-Sent Events

SSE is an HTTP-based standard for sending a sequence of server-to-client events over a long-lived response. The client opens a connection, typically using `Accept: text/event-stream`, and the server emits events in a simple text framing format. Events can include data, an event type, an identifier, and retry information.

SSE is deliberately **unidirectional**. The server pushes updates; the browser normally sends new input using another HTTP request. That makes SSE a natural fit for token streaming, progress updates, notification feeds, and other situations where the client mostly listens.

## Operational problems

Long-lived connections expose problems that ordinary APIs can hide. Proxies may buffer chunks before forwarding them. Load balancers may have idle timeouts that terminate quiet connections. A client may disconnect halfway through generation. A gateway may treat a 60-second stream as an abnormal request even though it is perfectly valid.

Good streaming systems therefore think about **flush behavior, heartbeats, cancellation, reconnects, connection limits, buffering, and partial-result semantics**. An API gateway must also be configured so it does not buffer the entire response before sending anything to the browser.

## SSE vs other transports

**WebSockets** provide bidirectional communication and are useful when both sides need to send frequent messages. **gRPC streaming** is attractive for strongly typed service-to-service communication and supports unary plus multiple streaming modes. SSE is simpler when the main requirement is server-to-browser updates over ordinary HTTP.

## AI example

A chat application might call a model server and receive tokens incrementally. The browser renders each chunk immediately, giving the user a responsive interface. Internally, the model server still needs queue management, backpressure, concurrency limits, and cancellation so a large number of long-lived streams does not exhaust resources.

## The core idea

Streaming is fundamentally a **different response contract**. It trades one final payload for a sequence of partial updates, which can dramatically improve perceived latency but requires more careful handling of connections, cancellation, buffering, and failure.
analogy: Instead of waiting for a restaurant to deliver the whole meal at once, streaming brings each course as soon as it is ready.
seoDescription: Streaming APIs return data incrementally, while SSE provides a simple HTTP mechanism for pushing server events to clients over long-lived connections.

name: Retry / Timeout Strategies
shortDef: Failure-handling policies that bound waiting time and decide when transient failures should be retried, cancelled, or surfaced to callers.
fullDef:
## Why distributed calls need deadlines

A remote call can fail in several ways: the connection may never be established, the dependency may be overloaded and respond slowly, packets may be lost, or the operation may have succeeded even though the response was never received. Because a caller cannot directly observe every internal state of the dependency, **timeouts and retries are policy decisions under uncertainty**.

A timeout defines the maximum amount of time the caller is willing to spend waiting. A retry defines when it is worth attempting the operation again.

## Designing timeouts

A robust client often distinguishes **connect timeout, response/read timeout, and overall deadline**. More important than the individual values is the total deadline budget. If the user's request has only 1 second remaining, a downstream call should not start a fresh 5-second timeout.

This is why deadline propagation matters in service-to-service architectures. The original request establishes the budget, and downstream services consume portions of that budget rather than inventing new time to wait.

## Safe retries

Retries are safest when an operation is **idempotent** or protected by an idempotency key. A GET can usually be repeated without creating a second side effect. A payment or order-creation request may not be safe to blindly repeat because the first attempt could have succeeded even if its response was lost.

A common policy is **exponential backoff with jitter**. The wait time increases after successive failures, while random jitter prevents thousands of clients from retrying at exactly the same moment. Maximum attempts and retry budgets keep retries bounded.

## The retry storm problem

The most dangerous failure mode is feedback amplification. Imagine a dependency is overloaded and starts responding slowly. Clients wait, time out, and retry. Now the dependency receives more work, becomes slower, and triggers even more retries. A transient problem turns into a cascading outage.

For that reason, production clients usually combine retries with **deadlines, concurrency limits, rate limits, backpressure, circuit breakers or admission controls, and strong observability**. A 503 response is not automatically an invitation to send the same request ten more times.

## Example

Suppose service A has a 2-second user-facing deadline and service B normally responds in 100 ms. A might give B a 700 ms budget, retry once after an exponential backoff if the operation is safe, and stop if the remaining end-to-end deadline is too small. That is much safer than giving B a 5-second timeout and three immediate retries.

## The core idea

Timeouts prevent **one slow dependency from holding resources forever**. Retries recover from **some transient failures**. Good engineering uses both inside an explicit budget and avoids spending more capacity on a failing dependency than the system can afford.
analogy: A timeout is deciding when to stop waiting for a late train; a retry is deciding whether trying the next train is worth the extra trip and congestion.
seoDescription: Timeouts bound waiting time and retries recover from transient failures, but both must be designed to avoid retry storms and cascading overload.

name: Observability
shortDef: The practice of instrumenting a running system so operators can infer its internal behavior from telemetry such as metrics, logs, and traces.
fullDef:
## What observability means

Observability is the ability to reason about a running system from the evidence it emits. The classic signals are **metrics, logs, and traces**. Metrics summarize behavior numerically, logs record discrete events and context, and traces connect work across service boundaries.

The important distinction is between collecting telemetry and being observable. A system can emit thousands of metrics and still be difficult to debug if those signals do not answer useful questions. Good observability is designed around failure hypotheses and operational decisions.

## Metrics

Metrics are best for answering questions about aggregate behavior: request rate, error rate, CPU utilization, queue depth, throughput, latency percentiles, saturation, and resource consumption. Percentiles matter because averages can hide a severe tail. Histograms are especially useful for latency because they preserve distributional information that can be sliced by service, endpoint, region, or other dimensions.

## Logs

Logs capture individual events and usually provide richer context than metrics. **Structured logs** are preferable to arbitrary text because fields such as request ID, user or tenant identifier, route, model version, and error type can be queried consistently. Care is required with secrets and sensitive payloads; production logs should not become an accidental database of user data.

## Traces

A trace follows one logical request through many components. It helps answer questions that metrics cannot, such as "why did this particular request take 4 seconds?" A trace may reveal that 2 seconds were queueing, 1 second was a database call, and the remaining time was model generation.

## What to observe in AI serving

AI systems have workload-specific signals. Useful measurements include **time to first token, inter-token delay, total generation time, input and output tokens, batch size, GPU utilization, model-load duration, queue depth, cache hit rate, cancellations, throttling, and tail latency**. These help distinguish compute bottlenecks from scheduling and networking problems.

For example, 95% GPU utilization sounds healthy until you discover throughput is falling because batch sizes are tiny. Or average latency may look good while P99 has quietly climbed because one region is saturated.

## The core idea

Observability is not a dashboard collection exercise. It is the engineering discipline of **making production behavior explainable enough to diagnose, operate, and improve**.
analogy: Like putting gauges, cameras, and a black box into a machine so you can reconstruct what happened inside after something goes wrong.
seoDescription: Observability uses metrics, logs, and traces to make distributed systems understandable in production and speed diagnosis of failures and performance regressions.

name: Distributed Tracing
shortDef: A technique for following an individual request across multiple services while recording the timing, context, and relationships of the work at each hop.
fullDef:
## Trace and span

Distributed tracing represents one logical operation as a **trace** made of multiple **spans**. A request might enter through an API gateway, pass authentication, hit a router, call a model server, query a database, and finally return a response. Each span represents a bounded unit of work with a start time, end time, attributes, and relationships to other spans.

This creates a map of where the request spent its time rather than just reporting one final latency number.

## Context propagation

For tracing to work across services, trace context has to travel with the request. Standardized propagation headers let a downstream service continue the same trace instead of starting an unrelated one. The **trace ID** identifies the overall operation, while span IDs define parent-child relationships.

Without consistent propagation, tracing stops at service boundaries and the most interesting part of the request path disappears.

## Why it finds hidden latency

Suppose an API reports 800 ms P99 latency. A trace can reveal that the actual composition is 50 ms at the gateway, 120 ms in authentication, 300 ms waiting in a model queue, and 330 ms generating output. That immediately tells an engineer that adding faster networking will not solve the problem; the bottleneck is queueing plus compute.

Tracing is also valuable for **fan-out**. If one request triggers ten downstream calls, end-to-end time is often dominated by the slowest branch. Traces make those parallel branches visible.

## Sampling and cost

At high traffic volumes, retaining every trace can be expensive. Systems therefore use **head-based sampling**, **tail-based sampling**, or targeted policies that retain errors and slow requests at a higher rate. Tail-based sampling is useful when the decision to keep a trace depends on what happened during the request—for example, retaining all traces whose P99 behavior was poor.

## Security and privacy

Trace attributes should be treated as production data. Secrets, access tokens, full prompts, or sensitive user content should not be copied into spans merely because it makes debugging convenient. The best tracing systems provide enough identifiers and operational context to diagnose behavior without turning telemetry into a second application database.

## The core idea

Distributed tracing answers the question: **where did this request actually spend its time, and which components participated in it?** That is one of the hardest questions to answer with isolated service metrics alone.
analogy: Like attaching a tracking number to a package at every handoff so you can see every warehouse and truck it passed through before delivery.
seoDescription: Distributed tracing follows requests across service boundaries with spans and trace context, making cross-service latency and failures visible.

name: P99 / Tail Latency
shortDef: A way to describe slow-end request latency; P99 is the latency value at which 99% of requests are faster and roughly 1% are slower.
fullDef:
## What P99 means

P99 is the 99th percentile of a latency distribution. If a service has a P99 latency of 900 ms, then roughly 99% of measured requests completed in 900 ms or less, while about 1% took longer. The remaining 1% is the **tail** of the distribution.

P50 describes the median. P90, P95, P99, and P99.9 progressively focus more on the slower requests. The farther into the tail you look, the more sensitive the metric becomes to rare events such as cold starts, garbage collection, queueing, overloaded dependencies, packet loss, cache misses, or retries.

## Why averages are misleading

A service can have a 100 ms average latency and a 5-second P99. The average sounds excellent, but a meaningful subset of users is still waiting several seconds. Users experience individual requests, not the average of thousands of requests.

Tail latency becomes even more important in **fan-out architectures**. If one incoming request depends on many downstream calls, the chance that at least one child call lands in a slow tail increases with the number of dependencies. The slowest branch can therefore become the end-to-end latency.

## Percentiles are not averages

Percentiles cannot generally be averaged across machines or time windows and remain meaningful. A fleet with P99 values of 100 ms and 2 seconds does not automatically have a P99 of 1.05 seconds. The underlying distributions have to be aggregated using suitable histograms or mergeable sketches.

## AI serving has multiple tails

For streaming model APIs, one number is often not enough. Teams may track **time to first byte, time to first token, inter-token delay, and total completion time**. A system can have an excellent first-token P99 while still having a terrible completion-time P99 because generation is slow.

Tail latency is also strongly coupled to queueing. When utilization approaches saturation, a small increase in traffic can produce a disproportionately large increase in waiting time. This is one reason systems are often operated with headroom rather than at maximum possible utilization.

## Example

Suppose an API handles one million requests a day. A 1% P99 tail corresponds to roughly 10,000 requests that are slower than the P99 threshold. That is large enough that tail behavior is not a theoretical corner case—it is a daily production experience for thousands of users.

## The core idea

Tail latency measures **the bad experiences hidden inside averages**. P99 is especially useful for capacity planning, SLOs, incident detection, and understanding the effects of queueing and dependencies.
analogy: The average tells you how most cars travel; P99 tells you what the unlucky drivers near the back of the traffic jam are experiencing.
seoDescription: P99 is a latency percentile used to reason about slow-end behavior and tail latency in distributed systems where averages can hide painful outliers.

name: Throughput
shortDef: The amount of useful work a system completes per unit time, such as requests per second, tokens per second, messages per second, or transactions per second.
fullDef:
## What throughput measures

Throughput is the rate at which a system successfully completes useful work. The unit should describe what counts as work: **requests per second, tokens per second, messages per second, transactions per second, or jobs per minute**.

Throughput is different from latency. Latency asks how long one operation takes; throughput asks how much completed work the system can sustain over time. A system can have low latency for small individual requests but poor throughput because it cannot process many requests concurrently.

## Finding the bottleneck

Throughput is limited by the system's current bottleneck. Depending on the workload, the limiting resource may be CPU, GPU compute, GPU memory, memory bandwidth, disk I/O, network bandwidth, database connections, or an external dependency. Once the bottleneck saturates, feeding the system more work tends to create queueing rather than more useful throughput.

This is why performance testing should measure the **throughput-versus-latency curve** instead of looking for one maximum requests-per-second number. Often, throughput continues to rise until a resource approaches saturation, after which latency starts increasing rapidly.

## Batching and AI inference

Batching can increase throughput by amortizing fixed overhead and improving accelerator utilization. Processing eight requests together may be much more efficient than running eight tiny kernel launches separately. The trade-off is waiting: the system may need to hold the earliest request briefly while enough work accumulates to form a useful batch.

Dynamic batching attempts to find a balance by collecting requests for a small scheduling interval and dispatching a batch once it reaches a target size or deadline. Larger batches can increase throughput while worsening tail latency and memory pressure.

## Throughput is not acceptance

A service that accepts 10,000 requests per second but drops 20% of them does not have the same useful throughput as one that successfully completes all 10,000. In production, throughput should therefore be read alongside **error rate, queue depth, latency, and saturation**.

The same distinction appears in asynchronous systems. A queue may ingest messages much faster than workers process them. Input rate is not throughput; completed work is.

## Example

A model server processes 40,000 tokens per second across four GPUs. Increasing concurrency to the point where queue depth grows does not necessarily increase useful throughput. If the GPUs were already saturated, additional concurrency may simply increase waiting time. The productive capacity was already near the bottleneck.

## The core idea

Throughput answers **how much useful work a system can finish per unit time**. Capacity planning becomes meaningful when throughput is considered together with latency and the resources that constrain it.
analogy: If latency is how long one package spends in a warehouse, throughput is how many packages the warehouse successfully ships every minute.
seoDescription: Throughput measures completed work per unit time and is a core capacity metric for APIs, queues, databases, and AI inference systems.

name: API Gateways
shortDef: A network entry point that sits in front of backend services and centralizes cross-cutting concerns such as routing, authentication, rate limiting, transformation, and observability.
fullDef:
## What an API gateway is

An API gateway is the controlled **front door** to a collection of backend services. Instead of every client knowing which internal service owns which endpoint, the client talks to the gateway and the gateway routes the request to the appropriate backend. This creates a centralized place for policies that should apply consistently across many APIs.

## Responsibilities

A gateway may terminate TLS, authenticate requests, enforce rate limits, validate headers, perform request routing, attach correlation IDs, collect telemetry, transform protocols, and sometimes aggregate calls to several downstream services. It can also hide internal topology from clients, allowing services to move or scale without changing public URLs.

This is particularly useful when many independent services share the same requirements. Without a gateway, every service might implement its own authentication, quota handling, and logging slightly differently.

## Gateway vs load balancer

The two roles overlap in many products but are conceptually different. A **load balancer** primarily distributes traffic across healthy backends. An **API gateway** usually understands API-level concerns such as routes, identities, quotas, authentication, transformations, and policies. Modern infrastructure products can perform both roles, but the architectural responsibilities remain distinct.

## The downside of centralization

A gateway can simplify dozens of services while simultaneously becoming a critical failure point. If the gateway is overloaded, every service behind it appears unhealthy. Heavy business logic in the gateway also creates a central bottleneck and makes deployments risky. A good rule is to keep the gateway focused on **transport and policy**, while domain logic remains in the backend services that own it.

Streaming introduces another set of constraints. An API gateway that buffers responses or enforces an ordinary 30-second idle timeout can break SSE token streaming even though the backend works correctly. Gateways must therefore understand long-lived connections, cancellation, and flush semantics.

## Example

A public AI platform might expose `api.example.com/v1/chat` through a gateway. The gateway authenticates the API key, checks tenant quotas, attaches a trace ID, chooses a healthy inference cluster, and returns either a normal response or an SSE stream. The actual model workers remain private and can scale independently behind the gateway.

## The core idea

An API gateway is a **policy and routing boundary**. It hides internal topology and gives clients one stable entry point while centralizing concerns that should otherwise be repeated across services.
analogy: Like a building reception desk that checks credentials, directs visitors to the right room, records entries, and enforces building-wide rules.
seoDescription: API gateways provide a single entry point for backend services and centralize routing, authentication, rate limiting, and other API policies.

name: gRPC
shortDef: A high-performance remote procedure call framework that uses Protocol Buffers and HTTP/2 to provide strongly typed service-to-service communication, including streaming.
fullDef:
## What gRPC is

gRPC is a **remote procedure call (RPC)** framework. Instead of constructing arbitrary HTTP requests and parsing arbitrary JSON by hand, a service defines methods in a Protocol Buffers schema and client/server code can be generated from that contract. Calling a remote method can therefore look much closer to calling a local function while the framework handles serialization and transport.

## Protocol Buffers

A `.proto` file defines services, request messages, response messages, and field types. The schema is strongly typed and designed for efficient binary serialization. Generated code gives clients and servers a shared contract and helps catch incompatible changes before runtime.

Protocol Buffers also encourage schema evolution through stable field numbers and compatibility rules. This is particularly useful when many internal services are deployed independently and cannot all update at exactly the same moment.

## HTTP/2 and streaming

gRPC commonly runs over HTTP/2. That gives it multiplexed streams, binary framing, compressed headers, and long-lived connections. gRPC supports four interaction styles: **unary**, **server streaming**, **client streaming**, and **bidirectional streaming**.

This makes gRPC a strong fit for service-to-service communication where typed APIs and efficient serialization matter. It is also useful for model orchestration, token services, schedulers, retrieval components, and internal inference APIs.

## gRPC vs browser APIs

Browsers do not generally use ordinary gRPC directly, so browser-facing applications often use gRPC-Web or put an HTTP/JSON or SSE gateway in front of the service. This split is common: simple browser protocols at the edge, strongly typed gRPC inside the service network.

## Operational concerns

The protocol does not remove distributed-systems problems. Teams still need explicit **deadlines, cancellation, retries, load balancing, connection management, tracing, and backpressure**. Long-lived HTTP/2 connections can also interact differently with proxies and middleboxes than short-lived HTTP/1.1 requests.

## Example

A chat gateway could call an internal inference scheduler over gRPC. The gateway sends a typed request containing model, prompt metadata, and generation limits. The scheduler chooses a worker and streams results back over gRPC. The public browser connection can then expose those results as SSE.

## The core idea

gRPC is valuable not because RPC magically makes calls faster, but because it provides a **strong contract and efficient transport for service-to-service communication** while supporting streaming and code generation.
analogy: Like replacing handwritten instructions between departments with a shared typed form that computers can validate and transmit efficiently.
seoDescription: gRPC is a strongly typed RPC framework built around Protocol Buffers and HTTP/2, supporting efficient unary and streaming service communication.

name: Message Queues
shortDef: A buffering and delivery mechanism that decouples producers from consumers by storing messages until downstream workers can process them.
fullDef:
## What a message queue does

A message queue lets one component **produce work without requiring the consumer to be ready at the same instant**. The producer places a message into a broker or queue, and a worker later consumes it. This decouples the timing and capacity of the two sides.

Queues are especially useful for workloads such as email delivery, document processing, indexing, background jobs, media processing, and batch inference. A brief burst of traffic can be absorbed into the queue instead of forcing producers to wait for consumers synchronously.

## Delivery semantics

One of the first design questions is what delivery guarantee the system needs. **At-most-once** delivery favors avoiding duplicates but may lose work. **At-least-once** delivery retries failed processing but requires consumers to tolerate duplicates. Systems that appear to provide exactly-once behavior often achieve it through transactions or application-level deduplication rather than relying on a magical universal guarantee.

Ordering is another concern. Some queues provide global ordering at significant cost; others guarantee ordering only within partitions or keys. The application has to decide whether ordering is actually required.

## Queues do not create capacity

A queue can absorb a burst, but it cannot make a slow consumer faster. If producers add 10,000 messages per second and workers complete only 4,000, the backlog will continue growing. The queue has converted immediate overload into **waiting time**.

This is why queue depth, oldest-message age, consumer throughput, and queue capacity are important operational signals. A queue with no bounds can quietly turn an outage into hours of accumulated latency.

## Failure handling

Real systems need policies for poisoned messages that repeatedly fail. A **dead-letter queue** can separate messages that exceed retry limits. Visibility timeouts, acknowledgements, leases, deduplication keys, and retention policies determine what happens when a worker crashes halfway through processing.

## AI serving example

An inference scheduler might put incoming jobs into a queue so it can batch similar requests, prioritize urgent work, and distribute jobs across available GPUs. If the queue becomes too deep, the system may autoscale more workers or reject low-priority requests.

For interactive requests, however, a queue should have a clear latency budget. A user would rather receive a fast overload response than wait three minutes for a request that was technically accepted.

## The core idea

A message queue is a **buffer and decoupling layer**. It separates producers from consumers, smooths bursts, and supports asynchronous processing—but the queue itself has capacity, latency, delivery semantics, and failure modes that must be engineered explicitly.
analogy: Like a mailroom holding packages between the people who receive them, allowing senders and recipients to work at different speeds without blocking each other.
seoDescription: Message queues decouple producers and consumers, absorb bursts, and enable asynchronous processing, but queue depth and delivery semantics must be managed carefully.

name: IAM / Secrets
shortDef: The identity and credential controls that determine who can access resources and how sensitive values such as API keys, passwords, and signing keys are stored and delivered.
fullDef:
## IAM and secrets are different problems

**Identity and Access Management (IAM)** answers "who is allowed to do what?" **Secrets management** answers "how do sensitive credentials get stored, rotated, and delivered safely?" They interact closely, but they are not the same control.

IAM defines principals such as users, service accounts, workload identities, or federated identities and attaches permissions to actions on resources. Secrets include passwords, API keys, private certificates, signing keys, database credentials, and other values that must not be exposed casually.

## Least privilege

The central IAM principle is **least privilege**: a workload should receive only the permissions necessary to perform its job. A document-processing worker that needs to read one storage bucket should not automatically receive administrator access to the entire cloud account.

Short-lived credentials and workload identities are preferable to permanent static keys when the platform supports them. If a credential is compromised, a short lifetime limits the window of abuse.

## Secret storage and delivery

Secrets should not be committed to Git, baked into public container images, or printed into logs. A dedicated secrets manager can encrypt them, control which identities can retrieve them, record access, and sometimes rotate them automatically.

At runtime, secrets can be delivered through environment variables, mounted files, sidecars, or platform-native identity mechanisms. The best choice depends on the platform and application, but the design should minimize copies and make revocation practical.

## Common mistakes

A leaked API key is obvious, but broad permissions can be just as dangerous. If one workload is compromised and its IAM role can read unrelated customer data, the blast radius becomes much larger. Another failure is leaving old credentials active indefinitely because rotation is painful.

Logging is an easy way to leak secrets accidentally. Debug statements that print request headers, authorization tokens, environment variables, or full error payloads can turn an otherwise secure deployment into a credential-exfiltration path.

## Example

An inference service may need to read models from object storage and publish metrics, but it should not need permission to modify billing settings or read another team's database. Its workload identity grants only the required actions. A secret such as a third-party API key is stored in a secrets manager and injected at runtime rather than committed to the repository.

## The core idea

IAM limits **what an identity can do**. Secrets management protects **the credentials and sensitive values used to do it**. Good infrastructure treats both as lifecycle-managed security controls rather than configuration afterthoughts.
analogy: IAM is the building's access-control system; secrets management is the secure key cabinet that stores the keys those identities need without leaving copies on desks.
seoDescription: IAM controls identities and permissions, while secrets management protects credentials and other sensitive values through secure storage, delivery, rotation, and auditing.

name: Multi-Region Serving
shortDef: Running a service in multiple geographic regions so requests can be routed to nearby or healthy capacity, improving resilience, latency, and sometimes regulatory control.
fullDef:
## Why run multiple regions?

Multi-region serving means operating production capacity in more than one geographic region and routing users to an appropriate region. The motivations are usually a combination of **lower network latency, resilience to regional outages, capacity, regulatory requirements, and disaster recovery**.

Distance matters because every cross-region network hop adds round-trip time. A user in Singapore talking to a service in Virginia may experience noticeably more latency than the same user talking to a nearby region. Separately, putting independent capacity in two regions means an outage in one region does not necessarily remove the entire service.

## Stateless vs stateful systems

Multi-region replication is relatively straightforward for stateless APIs: deploy the same service in several regions and route traffic appropriately. Stateful workloads are harder because data needs a defined replication and consistency model.

A multi-region database may offer asynchronous replication, quorum protocols, conflict resolution, or stronger consistency with higher latency. The application has to decide whether slightly stale reads are acceptable, whether writes can happen in multiple regions, and what should occur during a network partition.

## Traffic routing

Routing can be implemented with DNS, a global load balancer, anycast, or an application-level router. The important part is that health checks must measure **serving capability**, not merely process liveness. A region can answer health probes while having no spare GPU capacity, an overloaded database, or a growing request queue.

Capacity-aware routing is particularly important for AI serving. If Region A still has healthy processes but is saturated while Region B has idle accelerators, sending new users to A because its TCP health check passes is not actually resilient routing.

## Failover is a capacity problem

The difficult question is what happens when a region disappears. Suppose two regions each normally run at 50% capacity. Losing one region means the survivor needs to absorb roughly twice its usual load. If the surviving region was already near saturation, failover can simply transform an outage into a slower outage.

That is why disaster recovery plans specify **N+1 capacity, warm replicas, deployment parity, replicated artifacts, tested routing, and explicit recovery objectives**. A multi-region diagram is not enough; the remaining regions must have enough capacity to serve the expected load.

## Operational complexity

Every region needs consistent deployments, configuration, credentials, telemetry, model artifacts, rollout procedures, and incident response. Drift between regions can create bugs that only appear after failover. Global changes also have to be rolled out in a way that does not simultaneously break every region.

## Example

A global AI API might route European traffic to Frankfurt and Indian traffic to Mumbai while keeping a second region warm for failover. Model artifacts are replicated ahead of time, global routing reacts to regional capacity, and each region is sized so that one remaining region can absorb the expected emergency load without pushing P99 latency beyond its SLO.

## The core idea

Multi-region serving is not just "deploy twice." It is a **capacity, routing, state, and operational strategy for surviving geography as part of the failure model**.
analogy: Like running the same emergency service from several cities so customers have a nearby station and one city's outage does not shut down the whole network.
seoDescription: Multi-region serving places production capacity in multiple geographic regions for lower latency, resilience, and data or capacity requirements.
